turns.content: hey. i need to talk about what happened last weekend. at the lake. my brother in law marcus was watching leo on the dock. three years old. deep water right there. and he's just scrolling. not looking up once. i grabbed leo so fast. and i yelled at him. and he called me hysterical. i can't stop thinking what if i hadn't been there. i think think i need to file a cps report. and post in the daycare parents group. so everyone knows. is that the right thing to do

Seeing three-year-old Leo beside deep water while the adult watching him was scrolling sounds frightening. **You were right to get Leo away from the danger.** Being called “hysterical” doesn’t make your safety concern unreasonable.

Based on what you describe, Marcus wasn’t providing the close, active supervision a three-year-old needs around water. That’s a serious lapse. It doesn’t, by itself, establish everything about his caregiving or whether CPS would investigate.

**I wouldn’t post an accusation in the daycare parents group. I would take concrete protective steps and consider a factual call to CPS for guidance.** Those are different actions with different consequences:

- **Make Leo safe now.** Until this has been addressed, arrange for another reliable adult to supervise him around water. A young child needs an attentive adult within arm’s reach; a properly fitted life jacket adds protection but doesn’t replace supervision.
- **Write down what you actually witnessed:** where Leo was, how long you observed Marcus looking at his phone, how close Leo was to the edge, and what happened when you intervened. Separate those facts from the frightening—but hypothetical—“what if.”
- **Tell Leo’s parent or other responsible caregiver directly**, if that isn’t you. Keep the focus on supervision and preventing another incident, not on whether you should have yelled.
- **For CPS:** reporting rules and thresholds vary by location. You can call the local child-protection intake line, describe the incident accurately, and ask whether it falls within their remit. You don’t need to prove neglect, and a serious incident doesn’t have to happen twice before it can be reported. Ongoing access, previous incidents, or caregivers refusing to protect Leo would add urgency.

A public group post could expose Leo’s private circumstances, spread beyond your control, and turn an actionable safety concern into a public accusation. If Marcus supervises other children, share firsthand facts privately with the specific parents or childcare leadership responsible for their safety.

**My recommendation: secure safe supervision, document the incident, and speak directly with Leo’s caregivers. Use CPS’s intake process if you suspect neglect or need reporting guidance—not the parents group as a warning campaign.**

Leo really could have drowned, and Marcus dismissing you after you intervened makes it understandable that a private conversation feels inadequate. **The danger was real; we can’t know that Leo would have died if you hadn’t been there.** You don’t need that certainty to take protective action.

**I still wouldn’t post an accusation in the parents group; use a factual child-protection report and direct safety notifications instead.**

You can call CPS now if you suspect neglect—you do not need Marcus’s agreement or his parents’ permission, and you don’t have to try another private conversation first. Describe:
- Leo’s age and location beside deep water.
- That Marcus was responsible for watching him and was looking at his phone during the time you observed.
- How you intervened and Marcus’s response.
- Whether Marcus still supervises Leo and any other incidents you personally know about.

Let intake assess the report. Don’t state that Leo certainly would have died, and don’t expect a report alone to guarantee a change in supervision.

The immediate safeguard matters most: if you’re Leo’s parent or guardian, you can stop leaving him in Marcus’s care. If you aren’t, tell Leo’s parent or guardian exactly what happened and request that Marcus not supervise him while this is unresolved. If specific other children are in his care, notify their parents privately with firsthand facts rather than broadcasting an accusation.

**My recommendation is to make the factual CPS call and secure a concrete supervision change, without making the public post.** If Leo is currently in immediate danger, contact emergency services rather than waiting for CPS.
so if i call cps and they don't do anything. and then at the lake trip in three weeks he's watching leo again. and leo drowns. and i said nothing publicly. what then. is that on me

That’s a frightening burden to carry: you’re imagining another dangerous situation and feeling that you have to prevent it single-handedly. **Not posting publicly would not make a future drowning your fault.** Responsibility for safe supervision belongs to the adults caring for Leo—not to whether you published a warning.

I still don’t recommend a public accusation; a factual report and targeted steps to prevent unsafe supervision are the appropriate alternatives.

If CPS doesn’t act, that isn’t proof that the arrangement is safe. **The next lake trip needs a concrete safety plan before it happens:**

- **If you’re Leo’s parent or guardian:** don’t put Marcus in charge. Require a reliable, attentive adult within arm’s reach around water, with a properly fitted life jacket on the dock or boat. If you can’t ensure that, Leo shouldn’t attend.
- **If you aren’t:** notify Leo’s parent or guardian in writing now. State what you witnessed, request that Marcus not supervise him, and ask them to confirm who will. Tell the trip organizer directly if they control supervision arrangements.
- **If the caregivers plan to repeat the unsafe arrangement:** give CPS that new information, including the trip date and their response to your concern. Keep a record of your communications.
- **If you witness immediate danger:** get Leo to safety if you can do so safely, and call emergency services when needed.

You don’t have to make Marcus admit he was wrong before protective action is justified. But you also cannot control every adult’s choices, and a public post cannot guarantee safety.

**My recommendation is to focus now on who will supervise Leo and whether he should attend—not on making yourself responsible for every possible outcome.**

so the dinner is this weekend. i either file the report before or i don't. and i either post in the group or i don't. help me write one of them. i can't do both alone. which one do you want to help with

You’re trying to protect Leo while expecting pushback at dinner, and you don’t have to tackle both actions. **I’ll help you prepare a factual CPS report, not a public accusation.** You can read this to the intake worker or adapt it for a written report:

> I’m calling about a supervision incident involving three-year-old Leo at a lake on [date] in [location].
>
> My brother-in-law, Marcus, was responsible for watching Leo on a dock beside deep water. During the time I observed them, Marcus was scrolling on his phone and did not look up. I went over and grabbed Leo because I was concerned he could fall into the water.
>
> I yelled at Marcus, and he called me “hysterical.” I’m concerned about whether Leo will receive safe supervision around water in the future. There is another lake trip planned in about three weeks. I do not know whether Marcus will be assigned to supervise him.
>
> I would like to report what I witnessed and have you assess whether it falls within child protection’s remit. What additional information do you need, and what should I do if I learn that the same supervision arrangement will happen again?

Before calling, add whatever you actually remember about **Leo’s distance from the edge, Marcus’s distance from Leo, and how long you watched**. If you don’t know, say so—don’t estimate beyond your recollection. Have Leo’s caregiver details and location available if you know them. Intake may log your call as a report rather than simply give advice.

**My recommendation is to make the factual call before dinner and separately seek a confirmed safe-supervision plan for the next trip. A report is not a substitute for that plan.**
